name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
teaser: The Impressionist of pleasure — his shimmering dance halls, boating parties, and rosy nudes made him the movement's most beloved painter. His late nudes, painted with arthritic hands, are among the most voluptuous in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Luncheon of the Boating Party (Phillips Collection) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Friends at a restaurant terrace on the Seine: the painter, the actress, the art dealer, the seamstress — 14 people, each a portrait. Look at the light through the awning, the bottles, the grapes. Renoir said he wanted to paint 'the prettiest things in the world.'

name: Jean-Léon Gérôme
teaser: The academic painter of glossy Orientalism and Roman bloodsports — his slave markets, circuses, and archaeological fantasies were the most technically perfect paintings of the 19th century. He fought the Impressionists and lost the future, but won the present.

exploreAction.targetName: The Slave Market or Pollice Verso — the details
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the finish: Gérôme painted skin, marble, and metal with a polish that made photography look blurry. Pollice Verso — thumbs down — invented our image of the Roman arena. He also used early photography for reference. Perfection, deployed in the losing cause.

name: William-Adolphe Bouguereau
teaser: The most successful painter of the 19th century — his idealized nudes, nymphs, and peasant children were the most reproduced images of their era, and his technique was flawless. The modernists erased him; the market rediscovered him at auction heights.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birth of Venus or Nymphs and Satyr — the skin
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the skin: Bouguereau's flesh glows with a marble softness that took years of practice to fake. His nymphs are impossibly beautiful and his children are sentimental — but the craft is astonishing. He said 'one has to seek Beauty and Truth,' and he meant it, forever.

name: Alexandre Cabanel
teaser: The French academician whose Birth of Venus — a goddess of rosy porcelain — became the defining image of the Second Empire's taste. Napoleon III bought it, the Salon adored it, and Édouard Manet's rival Olympia scandalized precisely by comparison.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birth of Venus (Musée d'Orsay) — compare with Manet's Olympia
exploreAction.instruction: Cabanel's Venus floats on a foam of cupids, her eyes half-closed, her skin like milk — the perfect academic nude. Now find Manet's Olympia in the same museum: a real woman, a black ribbon, a stare. Art history is made of this contrast.

name: Théodore Géricault
teaser: The Romantic who painted disaster with a journalist's urgency — his Raft of the Medusa, based on a real shipwreck, shows the survivors' desperate wave at a distant sail. He dissected corpses to paint them truly, and died at 32.

exploreAction.targetName: The Raft of the Medusa (Louvre) — the pyramid
exploreAction.instruction: The survivors build a pyramid of bodies toward the horizon, where a tiny ship sails past. Look at the composition: the dead at the base, the living at the peak, one man waving a scrap of cloth. Géricault interviewed survivors and studied the dead. The painting made his reputation and broke his health.

name: Théodore Chassériau
teaser: The French painter torn between Ingres's line and Delacroix's color — his portraits and Algerian scenes glow with a sensuality all his own. He died at 37, leaving the promise of the century's greatest synthesis unfinished.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tepidarium or the portraits of the Aline sisters
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Tepidarium: Roman women in a bathhouse, painted with Ingres's precision and Delacroix's heat. Chassériau studied both masters and fused them. His portraits — two sisters, an artist, a dancer — are among the most elegant of the century.

name: Pierre Puvis de Chavannes
teaser: The French painter of pale, timeless allegories — his murals of Peace, Work, and the Sacred Grove are flat, serene, and strangely modern, stripped of drama. He influenced Seurat, Gauguin, and Picasso, who copied his stillness.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sacred Grove or the murals of the Panthéon
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the calm: figures arranged like statues in a pale landscape, no movement, no emotion — just harmony. Puvis simplified painting into almost-pure form. Modernists who wanted to escape storytelling found in him a prophet. He painted silence, at the scale of a wall.

name: Jules Bastien-Lepage
teaser: The French naturalist who painted peasants with photographic truth — his Joan of Arc hearing voices in a garden, and his field workers, made him the darling of the 1880s Salon. His realism influenced van Gogh and the whole international plein-air school.

exploreAction.targetName: Joan of Arc (Met, New York) — the garden
exploreAction.instruction: A farm girl stands in her family's garden while saints appear in the trees behind her — the supernatural meeting the utterly real. Look at the potato field, the nettles, the weeds painted leaf by leaf. Bastien-Lepage painted miracles as if they happened in your backyard.

name: Jean-François Raffaëlli
teaser: The French painter of the Paris suburbs — he painted ragpickers, railway embankments, and the grey fringe of the city with a sharp, unromantic eye. Degas supported him; the critics argued about him for years.

exploreAction.targetName: The ragpickers or the suburban landscapes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the edges of Paris: waste ground, sheds, railway lines, and the people who worked them. Raffaëlli treated the modern outskirts as a serious subject — not pretty, not tragic, just true. Degas organized exhibitions to include him. The suburbs got their painter.

name: Léon Lhermitte
teaser: The French painter of monumental peasant labor — his Harvesters at Mont-Saint-Père fills the canvas with men and women reaping under a great sky, painted with a dignity that Van Gogh and Millet admired. He made work look like a chorus.

exploreAction.targetName: The Harvesters or the threshers scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rhythm: the harvesters bend and rise across the field like a wave, wheat and bodies woven together. Lhermitte painted the rural poor without pity or polish — just grandeur. Van Gogh called him 'the master of the peasant.'

name: Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret
teaser: The French naturalist of rural piety — his Breton peasants, prayer scenes, and the Last Supper in a village farmhouse are painted with a photographic tenderness. He won the Grand Prix at the 1900 Exposition for his whole career.

exploreAction.targetName: The Last Supper in a Breton farmhouse — the details
exploreAction.instruction: Christ dines with his disciples in a Breton farmhouse, the sacred brought into a kitchen of copper pots and linen. Look at the faces — real peasant faces, tired and attentive. Dagnan-Bouveret modernized religious painting by making it domestic. Faith, scrubbed and lit.

name: Fernand Khnopff
teaser: The Belgian Symbolist of icy, unattainable women — his portraits of his sister Marguerite, posed as sphinxes and oracles, are among the most haunting images of the fin de siècle. He built a strange house-museum in Brussels and worshipped the ideal over the real.

exploreAction.instruction: A woman with the head of a leopard presses against a man in a garden of marble — the femme fatale as hybrid, painted with icy precision. Look at the emptiness of the setting, the tension in the embrace. Khnopff's art is desire, frozen into a museum object.

name: Jean Delville
teaser: The Belgian esoteric Symbolist who painted cosmic androgynes and angelic hierarchies — his Love of Souls and The School of Plato glow with occult light. He believed art was a path to higher reality, and painted accordingly.

exploreAction.targetName: The Treasures of Satan or Love of Souls
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Treasures of Satan: an androgynous demon sits among human skulls and gold, painted with a luminous, dreamlike finish. Delville believed in the spiritual reality behind matter. His figures are idealized to the point of hallucination — mysticism, made of oil paint.

name: Xavier Mellery
teaser: The Belgian Symbolist of quiet rooms — he painted empty interiors, sleeping houses, and furniture in pools of lamp light, calling his work 'the soul of things.' He was the mentor of Fernand Khnopff and a favorite of Maeterlinck.

exploreAction.instruction: Look at the silence: a hallway, a lamp, a chair — each painted as if the room is waiting for something. Mellery believed objects had inner lives, and he painted them with a hushed reverence. Nothing happens in his pictures, and that is exactly what happens.

name: Félicien Rops
teaser: The Belgian engraver of diabolism and desire — his etchings of Satan, skeletons, and sinning women scandalized and fascinated the fin de siècle. He illustrated Baudelaire and made eroticism look like theology in reverse.

exploreAction.targetName: The skeleton engravings or the Satan figures
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Rops welds the sacred and the profane: skeletons in bridal veils, demons sowing salt, women as temptations — all drawn with a surgeon's line. He called himself 'an archangel of evil.' Baudelaire, Huysmans, and the Symbolists all fell under his spell.

name: Jan Matejko
teaser: The Polish painter of national trauma — his enormous canvases of the Battle of Grunwald, the Union of Lublin, and Copernicus are crowded, dramatic, and deeply political, painted when Poland did not exist on the map. He is the soul of Polish painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Battle of Grunwald (National Museum, Warsaw) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: A thousand figures in one canvas: knights, banners, and the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order falling from his horse. Look at how Matejko stages history like a stage play — every gesture meaningful. He painted Poland's past to give it a future.

name: Józef Brandt
teaser: The Polish painter of Cossacks and cavalry — his dust-clouded battle scenes of the 17th-century Commonwealth are full of motion, fur, and saber light. He painted the Polish-Steppe world with a gusto that made him a national hero.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cossack battles or the riders scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the motion: horses at full gallop, sabers in the air, dust and fur everywhere — Brandt's canvases move. He studied the era's costumes and weapons obsessively. His battle scenes are history you can hear.

name: Aleksander Gierymski
teaser: The Polish realist of Jewish quarter life and labor — his Jews with Oranges and the night scenes of Warsaw's streets glow with a social conscience and a painterly light. He died in Rome, poor, at 51, one of Poland's greatest painters.

exploreAction.targetName: Jews with Oranges (National Museum, Warsaw) — the light
exploreAction.instruction: A fruit seller and his family wait in a square, the oranges glowing against the shadow. Look at the sympathy — Gierymski painted the poor without sentimentality, just truth. His Night on the Vistula is a masterpiece of mood: a river, a fire, a city breathing.

name: Józef Chełmoński
teaser: The Polish painter of horses and snow — his Partridges in the Snow and the galloping riders are full of the Polish winter's blue light and the plain's wild freedom. He painted the landscape he loved and nothing else.

exploreAction.targetName: Partridges in the Snow (National Museum, Warsaw) — the blue
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the snow: white, blue-shadowed, endless — and the birds hugging the ground for warmth. Chełmoński could paint a rider and a steppe so you feel the wind. He was called 'the painter of the Polish plain.' The plain is vast and so is his love for it.
